title: Multi-role Workflows Are Fragmented
summary: This situation describes how complex software becomes fragmented when one interface must serve roles with different tasks, rhythms, physical settings, and consequence profiles. Creative Navy uses observed workarounds to distinguish interaction-level problems from architecture-level mismatches.
keyFacts: A single interface architecture can serve one role well while creating friction for roles with different task structures or operating rhythms.
The structural question is whether roles share a task model or require different interface architectures.
Task-specific workarounds indicate that a unified model may be improved at the interaction or hierarchy level.
Role-specific workarounds indicate that the architecture itself may be wrong for at least one role.
The two documented resolutions are a unified model or architectural separation.
Triopsis used a unified interface across three roles after 43 user interviews across 21 participants, three in-situ observation sessions, and 47 microtasks mapped against three personas.

Kardion MCS Controller used one clinical screen for roles positioned at approximately 3 metres and close to the controller, and received FDA approval with no design changes required during regulatory evaluation.
IDEXX Animana led to a recommendation for architectural separation after field research across 35 clinics, 150+ participants, and 3 countries.
Assemblio's operating-context material is client-stated; Creative Navy did not observe a shop floor.
Topera is a concept design grounded in the DIN 69901 series and ProSTEP iViP / VDA recommendations; it is not a built or deployed system.

bodySections.heading: Multi-role Workflow Fragmentation in Complex Software
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Multi-role workflow fragmentation is the condition in which one software interface serves several roles with different tasks, operating rhythms, or consequence profiles, causing some roles to rely on workarounds because the interface architecture does not match their operational reality.

A single interface architecture can serve one role well while creating friction for another. The fragmentation often accumulates as a product is built around one role's mental model, extended for another role, and patched for a third.

The operational cost becomes difficult to see because users in underserved roles create workarounds. Those workarounds become habitual, and the gap between the designed interface and the interface actually used becomes normalised.

This situation is common in products where users share a system but not a task. Examples include enterprise SaaS platforms used by planners, operators, and field technicians; clinical devices used by surgeons and nurses from different physical positions; and practice management systems used by receptionists and clinicians in different operational modes.

bodySections.heading: Feature Additions Do Not Resolve Structural Role Fragmentation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Multi-role workflow fragmentation is not usually resolved by adding features for underserved roles or reorganising navigation. Those responses operate at the interaction level. The structural question is whether the roles share a task model that a single unified interface can satisfy, or whether their operating modes are different enough that one architecture will degrade at least one role.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats this as a classification problem before treating it as a design problem. Without that classification, design work can improve one role's experience while making another role's work harder.

The distinguishing signal is the pattern of workarounds. Task-specific workarounds, where multiple roles work around the same interface problem in similar ways, indicate that the interaction pattern or information hierarchy may need improvement. Role-specific workarounds, where each role develops distinct coping strategies, indicate that the interface architecture may be wrong.

bodySections.heading: Unified Model and Architectural Separation Are the Two Resolution Types
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A unified model is appropriate when roles share workflows but have different information priorities. The conflict is about what should be prominent, what should be accessible, and what order should govern the interface. In this case, the work is in information architecture and information hierarchy rather than in splitting the product.

Architectural separation is appropriate when roles operate in different modes with different physical environments, time structures, and consequence profiles. In this case, the problem is not hierarchy but task model. Separate interfaces for separate operating modes can be the correct design conclusion.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method uses Sandbox Experiments to map workflows before design decisions are made. Microtask analysis documents discrete tasks independently of assumed sequence or flow. Tension-driven reasoning then identifies whether the conflict between roles is interaction-level or architectural.

bodySections.heading: Triopsis Used One Model for Three Roles With Different Priorities
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Triopsis workforce management SaaS case, a single workforce management interface served schedulers, operations managers, and field technicians. Schedulers planned thousands of weekly interventions and coordinated crew availability. Operations managers scanned for exceptions and managed risk across broader time horizons. Field technicians performed tasks outdoors with gloves, in sunlight, under time pressure, and with interruption.

The roles had incompatible mental models at the interface level. A scheduler-oriented layout hid exception signals needed by operations managers. A structure that reassured field technicians by surfacing required steps and safety confirmations obscured timing data needed by planners.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treated those conflicts as evidence. Forty-three user interviews across twenty-one participants and three in-situ observation sessions showed that the roles shared the same workflow but operated it at different speeds, with different information priorities, and with different tolerance for uncertainty.

The resolution was a unified interface rather than separate products. Creative Navy mapped 47 microtasks against three personas and identified multi-role clarity at enterprise scale as the competitive vector. Product analytics from real users in the live system recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning.

bodySections.heading: Kardion MCS Controller Used One Screen for Physically Different Clinical Positions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Kardion MCS Controller case, two clinical groups used the same device screen during cardiac procedures and longer-term cardiogenic shock support. Scrub nurses and perfusionists stood approximately 3 metres from the controller during procedures while monitoring motor current and device positioning signals. ICU nurses worked close to the controller while monitoring flow rate, arterial blood pressure, and run time over longer care episodes.

The conflict was not only informational. It was spatial. A hierarchy optimised for surgical-distance reading would make elements visually dominant at close range. A hierarchy optimised for close-range nursing monitoring would make elements too small to read reliably from 3 metres under time pressure.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method resolved the conflict through a single screen hierarchy grounded in the observed choreography of clinical use. Elements needed at surgical distance were large enough to be legible at approximately 3 metres. The detail layer needed for close-range nursing monitoring remained present without dominating the screen at distance.

The Kardion MCS Controller received FDA approval, passing the regulatory evaluation as submitted with no design changes required. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

bodySections.heading: IDEXX Animana Required Architectural Separation Between Reception and Clinical Work
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
IDEXX Animana served reception staff and clinical staff through one interface for eleven years. Receptionists worked in an ambient awareness environment with simultaneous demands, short task windows, constant context-switching, and immediately visible error consequences for waiting clients. Clinical staff worked in focused, sequential case attention with clinical consequences attached to completeness and accuracy.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method classified this as an architecture-level mismatch. Field research across 35 clinics, 150+ participants, and 3 countries showed role-specific workarounds. Receptionists developed coping strategies for managing multiple animals per client at a glance. Clinical staff developed strategies for avoiding the clutter that a reception-oriented layout imposed on consultation screens.

The recommended resolution was architectural separation. The reception and clinical roles had different mental models of what the software was for, activated in different physical spaces and under different time structures. In this case, a unified interface optimised for either role would degrade the other.

bodySections.heading: The Industrial Automation Engagement Had Changing Roles Rather Than Fixed Personas
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
For a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells, role fragmentation appeared before role design could be fixed. Across customers, there were no defined roles. Each customer organised work differently, and the product had to adapt.

The field research identified five company archetypes, from a single-operator shop to a large corporation with eleven operator groups across six components. The engagement also showed that roles may change when staffing changes. If a setup operator leaves, a preset operator may need to perform both tasks and may not accept two computers for that combined work.

The design response described in the engagement is configurability by role group. An administrator selects the components a group needs, and that selection generates the group's navigation. The product is in development, not shipped, and these observations are not outcomes.

bodySections.heading: Assemblio Showed Fragmentation Caused by Component Reuse Across Incompatible Contexts
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Assemblio case, the Smart Viewer shop-floor application had been built from the Composer's components and looked almost identical to it, even though the requirements for the two user groups differed. The Composer user was an engineer or planner working at a desk with a mouse, keyboard, and desktop monitor.

Assemblio described the Smart Viewer user as a standing, gloved shop-floor worker in a bright, dirty, loud environment, with no guaranteed input devices. Some customers used foot pedals because both hands were occupied, and the device was usually a tablet on a holder.

The fragmentation had a traceable technical cause. The worker's product displayed the complete CAD hierarchy at all times, carried a view-orientation cube the worker did not need, and provided no route for a worker to send practical step feedback back to the planner.

Every statement about the shop-floor operating environment in this case is Assemblio's description. Creative Navy did not observe a shop floor, and no time-saving, error-rate, training, adoption, or engagement-date claim is established here.

bodySections.heading: Schone Airspace Group Used One Persistent Command Shell Across Role Contexts
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Schone Airspace Group mission control engagement, five operator role contexts were modelled as responsibilities within an operation: remote pilot, payload operator, mission planner, fleet supervising operator, and operations reviewer. The role contexts were not treated as a fixed staffing configuration because one person may hold several responsibilities on a small flight, while a larger operation may distribute them.

The resolution was not five tailored views. Creative Navy's design work held the role contexts together through one persistent live command shell with fixed positions for command target identity, last reported flight mode, battery, control link state, telemetry freshness, and consequential actions.

Workspace changes altered centre content, but not the location or meaning of the command region. The accepted cost was that the shell reserved screen space that could not be given to the map or video. The product is built and in test, not described here as operationally deployed.

bodySections.heading: Maritime Traffic Monitoring Treated Handover as the Point Where Fragmentation Becomes Risk
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In an engagement for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation, and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations, and waterway operators, unresolved work was spread across incident, alert, source-health, and workspace views. An operator had to assemble the active situation by cross-checking separate lists.

The designed response treated handover as an accountable review rather than a digest. The selected model grouped open alerts, source concerns, and incident tasks with owner, latest attributable event, and unresolved status, and required the receiving operator to review and accept.

This example shows how multi-role fragmentation can become a handover risk when active work is distributed across views and responsibility transfer is assumed rather than explicitly reviewed.

bodySections.heading: Topera Was Designed Against Fragmentation as a Concept, Not Observed as a Live System
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Topera is a concept design for a cross-organisational project management platform. It was grounded in the DIN 69901 series and the ProSTEP iViP / VDA recommendations. The engagement included no user research and no contact with any project manager or partner-organisation representative.

The information architecture was designed as a matrix with two axes. The horizontal time axis carried the five DIN 69901-2 lifecycle phases. The vertical knowledge axis carried eleven management domains. Both axes were designed as real routes rather than one primary navigation and one secondary navigation.

Topera was designed so roles in different organisations could hold different depths of the same plan. External partners were specified as asynchronous users with three to four structural levels exposed and no direct edit permissions. Internal users would see full depth. The boundary between those views was designed as part of the system structure rather than treated only as a permissions setting.

Nothing in the Topera example was observed in live use. Topera is not a built system, has no deployment, no users, no pilot, and no outcome claim.

strongClaims: Multi-role workflow fragmentation occurs when a single interface serves roles with different tasks, operating rhythms, or consequence profiles and creates workarounds for underserved roles.
The main diagnostic distinction is whether workarounds are task-specific or role-specific.
The two documented resolutions are unified model and architectural separation.

Triopsis used a unified interface across three roles after 43 user interviews, 21 participants, three in-situ observation sessions, and 47 mapped microtasks; live product analytics recorded 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning.

The Kardion MCS Controller used one screen hierarchy for clinical users at approximately 3 metres and close range, and the controller received FDA approval with no design changes required during regulatory evaluation.
IDEXX Animana was classified as requiring architectural separation after field research across 35 clinics, 150+ participants, and 3 countries showed role-specific workarounds.
weakerClaims: The industrial automation engagement identified five company archetypes, but the product is in development and no outcome is claimed.
Assemblio's fragmentation had a traceable technical cause in component reuse, but its shop-floor operating context was client-stated and not observed by Creative Navy.
Topera is a concept design against fragmentation, not a built system and not an observed research finding.
limitations: This page is a situation-level diagnostic page, not proof that one resolution type is always correct.
Triopsis outcome figures are limited to the live product analytics described in the current evidence and should not be generalised to other systems.
Kardion is described only with FDA approval wording; no FDA pathway is specified.
Assemblio's shop-floor operating context is client-stated and was not observed by Creative Navy.
The industrial automation product is in development, not shipped, and no outcome is established for that engagement.
Schone Airspace Group's product is built and in test, not described as operationally deployed.
Topera is a concept design with no built product, no deployment, no users, no pilot, no user research, and no outcome.
